items.title: Agentic Engineering Using Spec-Driven Development
items.text:
Abstract

This half-day workshop is designed to help development teams move beyond individual productivity gains to creating repeatable, institutional benefits with agentic coding tools. It emphasizes working effectively and responsibly by balancing human ownership and judgment with AI assistance to improve efficiency without sacrificing accountability. The workshop is structured around key phases of AI-driven engineering: requirements gathering, spec creation, implementation, and verification.

items.title: Workshop Flow
items.text:
1. Prerequisites: Clone the repo, install dependencies, run migrations and seed data
  2. Presentation: Slides structured around key phases of AI-driven engineering: requirements gathering, spec creation, implementation, and verification
  3. Module 0 (Optional): Get to Know Your Agentic Tool [30 mins]
  4. Module 1: Requirements Gathering [45 mins]
  5. Module 2: Spec Creation [45 mins]
  6. Module 3: Implementation [45 mins]
  7. Module 4: Verification [45 mins]

Info

This is a half-day workshop consisting of 4 full modules, plus an optional introductory module for those new to agentic tools.

items.title: The Problem
items.text: Agentic coding tools unlock remarkable speed, but without a deliberate approach, that speed comes at the cost of human ownership. As developers offload more decisions to the agent, projects become harder to understand, maintain, and trust. The goal of Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is to reclaim that ownership intelligently: establishing clear points in the workflow where the human retains control, while still allowing the agent maximum autonomy everywhere else. SDD is not about slowing down; it's about maximizing agent autonomy without sacrificing project trust or human ownership.

items.title: Module 0 (Optional): Get to Know Your Agentic Tool
items.text: A hands-on introduction to agentic coding tools, covering core features like tool use, context, and permissioning. Participants practice prompt crafting, mode switching, and MCP server connections.

items.title: Module 1: Requirements Gathering
items.text: Learn to translate vague product requests into precise engineering inputs. Participants use an agent to explore a brownfield codebase and surface constraints, unknowns, and clarifying questions.

items.title: Module 2: Spec Creation
items.text: Transform codebase understanding and product requirements into a structured development plan. Participants iterate with their agent to produce a spec that defines scope, validation criteria, and human feedback points.

items.title: Module 3: Implementation
items.text: Execute against a spec with the agent handling code changes autonomously. Participants practice calibrating their level of supervision, managing restarts, and refining iteratively using git as a safety net.

items.title: Module 4: Verification
items.text: Validate AI-generated output against technical and organizational standards. Participants combine human and AI-assisted review to assess risk, identify code smells, and make a ship/no-ship decision.

items.title: Modules
items.text: Module Topic Duration Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool Hands-on intro to agentic tools 30 mins (optional) Module 1: Requirements Gathering Understand the codebase and surface constraints 45 mins Module 2: Spec Creation Turn requirements into a structured development plan 45 mins Module 3: Implementation Spec-driven execution with the agent 45 mins Module 4: Verification Review, test, and make the risk call 45 mins

items.title: A Wordle Checker Script!
items.text:
wordle_check.py is a small program that scores a Wordle guess against a secret answer (🟩 green / 🟨 yellow / ⬜ gray). Copy and paste it into your IBM Bob editor.

You'll use this file to practice the mechanics of your agent: prompting, mode switching, built-in tools, and wiring up a simple GitHub MCP server.

wordle_check.py
"""
wordle_check.py — score a Wordle guess against the secret answer.

Given a 5-letter guess and the secret answer, return feedback for each
letter position:

    "green"  -> correct letter, correct position
    "yellow" -> letter is in the word, but a different position
    "gray"   -> letter is not in the word

Example:
    >>> score_guess("trace", "slate")
    ['yellow', 'gray', 'green', 'gray', 'green']
"""

WORD_LENGTH = 5

EMOJI = {"green": "\U0001F7E9", "yellow": "\U0001F7E8", "gray": "⬜"}


def score_guess(guess, answer):
    guess = guess.lower()
    answer = answer.lower()

    result = []
    for i in range(WORD_LENGTH):
        g = guess[i]
        if g == answer[i]:
            result.append("green")
        elif g in answer:
            result.append("yellow")
        else:
            result.append("gray")
    return result


def render(guess, answer):
    pattern = score_guess(guess, answer)
    squares = "".join(EMOJI[p] for p in pattern)
    return f"{guess.upper()}  {squares}"


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # A few sample rounds. The answer is SLATE.
    print(render("trace", "slate"))
    print(render("crane", "slate"))
    print(render("eerie", "slate"))
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 1. Two Kinds of Prompts
items.text:
Ask your agent about the file twice:

  • Lazy: "Does this look correct?"
  • Structured: "Walk through score_guess and check how it handles a guess that repeats a letter the answer only contains once. Give a concrete example."

Notice how differently the two prompts land. Which one surfaces a real problem?

Note

Both prompts should surface the bug, but the structured prompt will give you a far more useful response. The takeaway isn't specific to this file: the more precisely you define what you want the agent to check, the more useful its output will be.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 2. Test Out the Modes
items.text:
Bob 2.0 ships with 3 streamlined modes (Ask, Plan, Agent). Move through them in order and notice how the agent's behavior and available tools change at each step:

  • Ask: Map out the file. Have it explain the logic trace and pin down the bug.
  • Plan: Lock the implementation plan. Have it propose a fix (don't let it edit yet).
  • Agent: Implement. Have it apply the fix.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 3. Use the Built-in Tools (read + write + run)
items.text: Now prove the fix holds. Ask your agent to write a few test cases to a new file (including a guess with a repeated letter, e.g. guess EERIE, answer SLATE) and run it. Does the output match what real Wordle would show? Paste back the original version to watch the same test fail; that's the bug you just fixed.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: 4. Use the GitHub MCP Server (Optional)
items.text:
Setting up the GitHub MCP server for GitHub Enterprise

1. In Bob, go to Settings → MCP, search for GitHub, and click Install. Select your workspace as the installation scope.

2. Generate a PAT at github.ibm.com/settings/tokens/new with at minimum repo scope (or just check all).

3. Set the following:

  • PAT: paste your token from step 2
  • Hostname: https://github.ibm.com
  • Toolsets: repos,issues,pull_requests

4. Open .bob/mcp.json and change "command": "docker" to "command": "podman".

5. Verify the connection (optional)

Run this to confirm the server starts and your PAT is valid: 

echo '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2024-11-05","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"test","version":"0"}}}' | \
  podman run -i --rm \
    -e GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN=<token> \
    -e GITHUB_HOST=https://github.ibm.com \
    ghcr.io/github/github-mcp-server 2>&1 | head -4
You should see both: 
token scopes fetched for filtering   ← auth worked, PAT is valid
GitHub MCP Server running on stdio   ← server started cleanly
Any error on either line tells you exactly what's wrong (bad host format, bad token, network issue) without needing to debug a silent disconnect in Bob.

Your file lives on your machine, but the GitHub MCP can still reach out to GitHub for you:

  • Fetch the reference: pull the README from hbattu/wordle_kata via the GitHub MCP and confirm the correct rule for repeated letters. Compare it to what your agent found in step 1.

  • Stretch goal (if your GitHub token allows): fork hbattu/wordle_kata via the MCP and either file an issue describing the bug or open a PR with your fix. This is a reflection of the real open-source flow, driven entirely through the agent.
path: Module 0: Get to Know Your Agentic Tool

items.title: The Codebase
items.text:
Finch Financial is an internal operations console for a fictional neobank. The app is already running with the following functionality built:

  • Sign in via email and password (all users share the password Password123!)
  • Browse and filter customer accounts by status and name
  • Search and filter transactions across all accounts
  • View an account's detail page with transactions, memos, and audit log
  • RBAC: analysts see active and frozen accounts; supervisors can also see closed accounts. Only supervisors can add memos.

items.title: Your Task
items.text:
Pick one of the two product requests:

1. Freeze and unfreeze customer accounts when suspicious activity is detected.

An ops analyst notices Northgate Properties just sent a $280,000 wire to Cayman Holdings Ltd, with no prior history of transfers anywhere near that size. They can't freeze the account themselves (that requires a supervisor), so they flag it to their supervisor, who logs in and freezes the account with a reason.

2. Flag suspicious transactions for follow-up review, with a supervisor resolution workflow.

An analyst notices Tran Consulting Group has a series of rapid international wires in both directions. They flag a transaction with a reason. The flag appears in a queue. A supervisor reviews it and resolves it.

See product-requests.md for further details.

This is the requirements-gathering phase. Your job is to understand the ground your feature will land on, not to plan or write code yet. It is recommended to stay in Ask mode while you explore, so the agent can read the repo but not change it. Switch to Agent mode only at the end, to write your requirements.md.

Use the below as guiding principles to understand the codebase architecture, gather requirements and success criteria, and clarify any important questions related to your product requests.

items.title: 1. Locate the Territory
items.text:
Ask the agent which files, services, and endpoints your request would touch, and how a request flows between them.

"I want to build [your request]. Which files and endpoints are relevant, and how does a request flow between them?"

Keep it scoped. Map only the slice your feature actually touches, and avoid ingesting the whole repo.

items.title: 2. Learn from What Already Exists
items.text:
Find the feature already in the app that most resembles your request and have the agent walk you through how it works end to end.

"What existing feature is most similar to [your request]? Walk me through how it works, layer by layer."

Then assess the gap: what does the app already provide for your feature, and what's missing? Have the agent contrast the current implementation with what your request needs.

items.title: 3. Capture Constraints, Dependencies, and Unknowns
items.text:
Ask what rules and conventions your feature must respect (who's authorized, what's sensitive and must never leak, what's audited, whether the data model needs a migration, how the API shapes responses) and store that information.

Flag anything the code doesn't decide for you: those are your unknowns.

items.title: 4. Generate Clarifying Questions
items.text:
Ask the agent to draft the questions a product owner would need to answer before this could be built: the things the code cannot tell you (business rules, edge cases, desired behavior).

Leave them open. Don't settle them here; capture them as questions. Module 2 opens by having the agent interview you about exactly these, one at a time, and being on the answering end is what surfaces assumptions you didn't know you were making.

These questions are the seed of your Module 2 spec.

items.title: 5. Spot-check the Agent
items.text: Don't take the agent's word for it. Open one or two files it cited and confirm its claims yourself. Note where the agent was right, vague, or wrong.

items.title: 6. Define Your Validation Criteria (Most Important)
items.text:
Requirements aren't only about behavior; they're about how you'll prove the behavior is right. Before you leave this phase, define what "done and correct" looks like as criteria that are measurable, testable, and unambiguous. This is what Module 4 will verify against, so "it should work" won't cut it.

Ask the agent what the repo already gives you to validate against (e.g.the type system, the test setup, RBAC rules, audit-log guarantees) and use those to shape success criteria a test could actually check.

Tip

It could be helpful to distill everything you gathered into a short requirements.md. That file is your bridge to Module 2: a focused, verified brief is what turns into a meaningful spec.

Security note

Don't paste secrets into prompts or have the agent open .env.

items.title: Module 2: Spec Creation
items.text:
Continue in the same session as Module 1 and bring your requirements.md in as context. The exploration you just did is what lets the agent plan against real files and line numbers, rather than in the abstract.

The agent's autonomy goes up here. You'll draft in Plan mode, but the plan is yours. Requirements are the input; the spec is the output: the one document Module 3 will build from. Your job is to iterate with the agent until that document is right, before a line of code is written.

items.title: 1. Frame the Requirements
items.text:
Before you ask for a plan, pin down the inputs yourself, grounded in your requirements.md:

  • What the system should do (functional)
  • The constraints it must hold (security, performance, scale)
  • The edge cases and failure modes
  • What's explicitly out of scope

items.title: 2. Generate an Initial Plan
items.text:
Hand the agent your requirements and ask it to draft a development plan broken into phases. Treat this first draft as raw material: your starting point, not your spec.

"Using my requirements and notes, draft a phased implementation plan for [your request]. Don't write code yet."

items.title: 3. Own the Plan: Review and Cut
items.text:
Read every phase. Decide yourself what's necessary, what's bloat, and what doesn't belong. This is where ownership is won or lost: rubber-stamp the first draft and you've handed the agent your design. Cut, reorder, correct.

Check it both ways: is anything missing (a requirement or validation criterion from Module 1 with no step behind it), and is anything too vague? Reject non-steps like "implement X"; each phase should be concrete enough to act on and to test.

items.title: 4. Refine Until it Holds Together
items.text:
Iterate before you implement, by hand or with the agent's help:

  • Refine as you review: keep reading and correcting the spec yourself
  • Interview mode: have the agent question you about the spec, one decision at a time
  • Refine through execution: let it attempt a slice, then fix the spec with what you learn

"Interview me about this spec, one question at a time, on anything ambiguous or unspecified."

Tip

Stop at a minimum viable spec: one where you understand and accept the architectural decisions and their level of detail. Don't over-invest chasing perfect.

items.title: 5. Build in Validation and Checkpoints
items.text: For each phase, define how you'll know it's done (ideally something the agent can run on its own, like a test). Then mark the points where you need to pause for human judgment on things a test can't catch.

items.title: 6. Write it to spec.md
items.text:
That document is the output of this module and the core input to Module 3. If it's clear enough that someone else could implement from it, you're ready.

Tip

Keeping yourself in the loop through an interactive back-and-forth (where the agent questions you about your own spec) is the fastest way to catch gaps without quietly handing design decisions to the agent.

items.title: Module 3: Implementation
items.text:
Start a new session, then point your agent at the spec.md you created in the previous module, and begin your implementation with a minimal, yet comfortable level of intervention. You'll work in Agent mode.

The fresh context is deliberate. The spec is the handoff, and a cold start is what forces it to carry the work on its own. If the session still remembers your Module 2 interview, a spec with gaps in it will still produce good code, and you'll never find out.

Auto-Acceptance

This is the highest-autonomy phase: the spec does the thinking, the agent does the work. Safely enable auto-acceptance where you can, thinking about which commands are safe to be autonomously run by the agent, and which require more cautious, human decision-making. Do this work up-front, so you can then get out of the way and let the agent make progress.

items.title: 1. Set Your Guardrails Up Front
items.text: Decide before you start what the agent can run on its own and what needs your approval. Auto-accept the safe, reversible things (reads, edits, running tests); gate the risky or irreversible ones. Doing this up front is what lets you step back afterward.

items.title: 2. Hand it the Spec and Let it Run
items.text:
Point the agent at spec.md and let it implement with minimal intervention. Resist the urge to do it yourself: the point is to see a good spec carry the work.

"Implement this spec phase by phase. Run the tests for each phase before moving on."

items.title: 3. Supervise Dynamically
items.text: Expect it to run straight through rather than stopping between phases. Unless your spec named a point where it should pause, it will report each phase and keep going. Use its progress tracking to keep a view and spot-check as you go. Don't hover over every token (that defeats the purpose), but don't wave through large or risky changes either.

items.title: 4. If it Derails, Reset
items.text:
Editing the spec while the agent is working will usually throw it off. If it's going off the rails, or the spec turns out too weak, stop, fix the spec, and restart cleanly:

git restore .

That reverts every tracked file the agent touched and leaves your requirements.md and spec.md alone, because they're untracked. Two modules of work can't be destroyed by the undo.

Never git clean

That deletes untracked files, which is exactly where your requirements.md and spec.md live.

Tip

Little hands-on ownership here means more to verify next. Let the agent move fast, and plan to validate carefully in Module 4.

items.title: Module 4: Verification
items.text:
Setup: Work from the change you built in Module 3. Start with git diff --stat, which shows you the blast radius in one screen.

This is where ownership and trust climb back up: the agent generated the code, now you take responsibility for it. Bob is a verification tool (it helps you test and review), but the judgment is yours.

Verification has two flavors: testing and review. Neither is optional, especially the review, and especially on anything with shared ownership.

items.title: 1. Set Your Verification Gates
items.text: Before you look at the diff, decide what "good enough to ship" means for this change: correctness, security, performance, scalability. Those gates are the bar you'll hold the code to.

items.title: 2. Review it Yourself First
items.text:
Read the diff as the author, not a spectator: this is how you take ownership back from the agent. Watch for the classic AI code smells:

  • Dead code, hardcoded values, and half-finished abstractions
  • Missed edge cases and outdated library usage
  • "Lazy" shortcuts: less code instead of correct code
  • Locally correct but globally wrong: right in the file, wrong for the system

Sort what you find: structural gaps go back to the spec, content errors you fix, loose code you tighten.

items.title: 3. Check the Tests
items.text:
Run the suite, then ask the sharper question. Not "what percentage is covered" but which of your validation criteria have no test behind them:

"Which validation criteria in my requirements have no automated test covering them?"

Coverage gaps are where the bugs you didn't catch are hiding. Closing one is a good use of the time you have left.

items.title: 4. Run an AI-assisted Review
items.text:
Have Bob summarize the changes and flag concerns as a second set of eyes. Then do the part only you can: separate real issues from noise, and the things that need human judgment from the things an agent can settle. Bob assists; it doesn't sign off.

"Review this diff against my spec. Summarize what changed and flag anything risky, incomplete, or inconsistent."

The AI Review Ouroboros

The agent wrote this code, and now the same agent is reviewing it: the same assumptions and the same blind spots on both ends. Code can appear correct, pass its own review, and still be missing requirements entirely.

Notice what it doesn't raise. A diff review can only see what's there, never what was never written, so work that was skipped is invisible to it. Ask a differently-framed question and the gap reappears immediately. The quality of an AI review is bounded by the question a human thought to ask.

items.title: 5. Make the Risk Call
items.text:
Would this ship at your organization? Judge by blast radius (how much it can break) and use-case sensitivity (how much it matters if it does). Decide the review level it warrants.

Then get peer review, which is non-negotiable when ownership is shared. Swap with the person next to you and review each other's diff. It's the only point today where a human reviews AI-generated code they didn't commission, which is exactly what breaks the loop.

Tip

AI fits into your existing review and governance process; it doesn't replace it. End this module with code you'd put your name on.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
Complete these steps before the workshop to make sure your environment is ready.

The app runs on SQLite — an embedded database file, with no server and no containers. Setup is two commands.

items.title: 1. Install Tools
items.text:
macOS only — Install Homebrew (if you don't have it)

Step 1 — Check if Homebrew is already installed: 

brew --version
✅ If you see a version number (e.g. Homebrew 4.4.0) — you're done, skip this section.

❌ If you get command not found — continue below.

Step 2 — Install Xcode command line tools: 

xcode-select --install

Step 3 — Install Homebrew: 

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Step 4 — Set up Homebrew in your shell: 

echo 'eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.zprofile
eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"

Step 5 — Verify: 

brew --version
# Homebrew 4.4.0

items.title: Node.js 22+
items.text:
Node 22 or newer is required

The database driver ships prebuilt binaries for Node 22+. On older versions npm install will fail trying to compile it from source.

macOSLinux (Ubuntu/Debian)Windows 
brew install node@22
node --version

curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_22.x | sudo -E bash -
sudo apt-get install -y nodejs
node --version

Download and install from nodejs.org

items.title: Git
items.text:
macOSLinux (Ubuntu/Debian)Windows 
brew install git

sudo apt-get install git

Download and install from git-scm.com

items.title: 2. Clone and Set Up
items.text:
git clone https://github.com/hbattu73/finch-financial.git
cd finch-financial
npm run setup

npm run setup installs dependencies, creates api/.env with working defaults, creates the SQLite database, and seeds it with workshop data. No configuration is needed.

items.title: 3. Start the App
items.text:
npm run dev

This starts the API (port 3000) and the web app (port 5173) together, with their output colour-coded in one terminal. Stop both with Ctrl+C.

Open http://localhost:5173 and log in with any of the workshop credentials. All users share the password Password123!.

items.title: Verify It Works
items.text:
You should see:

  • A list of customer accounts with status badges
  • The ability to filter by account status and name
  • An account detail page with transactions, memos, and audit log

If you can browse accounts and view transactions, you're ready.

Reset data at any time

The seed script is idempotent. To restore the original workshop data at any point, run: 

npm run seed
To start completely fresh, delete the database file and re-run setup: 
rm api/finch.db
npm run setup

items.title: Next Steps
items.text: Proceed to the Presentation to get started.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
Both suites are standalone — no running server and no database setup. Backend tests run the Express app in-process with supertest against a fresh in-memory SQLite database per test file. Frontend tests mock fetch.

Your development data is never touched by a test run.

# Everything
npm test

# One workspace
npm test -w api
npm test -w web

# A specific file, or watch mode
npm test -w api -- accounts.test.ts
npm test -w api -- --watch

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text:
npm install fails building better-sqlite3

Almost always an out-of-date Node. Check your version: 

node --version
If it's below 22, install Node 22+ (see above) and re-run: 
npm run setup

Port 3000 or 5173 is already in use

Another process is holding the port. Find and stop it:

macOS / LinuxWindows 
lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill
lsof -ti:5173 | xargs kill

netstat -ano | findstr :3000
taskkill /PID <pid> /F

Alternatively, set a different API port in api/.env.

npm run dev says dependencies are not installed

Run the setup command first: 

npm run setup

Clone fails with an authentication error

If you see: 

remote: Password authentication is not available for Git operations.
remote: You must use a personal access token or SSH key.
Authenticate using one of the following:

  • SSH key (recommended) — Generate an SSH key and add it to your GitHub account
  • Personal access token — Create a personal access token and use it in place of your password when prompted
